llm_response.content:
Below is a complete empirical plan tailored to your setup and the sharp age-30 eligibility rule in Quebec.

1. Identification Strategy
- Primary: Difference-in-Discontinuities (RD-in-Differences) around age 30
  - Rationale: In Quebec before August 1989 there is a sharp increase in cash assistance at exactly age 30 for childless employable adults; after August 1989 the discontinuity disappears. With single-year-of-age microdata in the 1986 and 1991 Censuses, we can estimate the discontinuity in outcomes at age 30 in Quebec when the rule was in force (1986) and compare it to (i) the contemporaneous discontinuity in the rest of Canada (where no such rule exists) and (ii) the discontinuity in Quebec after the rule was abolished (1991). The difference-in-discontinuities framework differences out smooth life-cycle changes across ages as well as any spurious age-30 features common across provinces or time.
- Complementary: Event-study/DID using the LFS around the August 1, 1989 reform date
  - Rationale: The LFS provides monthly data to assess dynamics immediately around the reform, comparing 25–29 to 30–34 in Quebec relative to rest-of-Canada (ROC). This corroborates the Census-based RD-in-differences and provides a time-series validation that the age-30 gap closes after the policy is removed.

2. Treatment and Control
- Treatment variable
  - For the RD framework: Eligibility for the higher adult social assistance schedule at age 30 in Quebec when the rule exists. Operationalized as an indicator D = 1(age ≥ 30).
  - For reduced form: D × Quebec × Pre-abolition (1986) is the “treated at the cutoff” contrast; post-abolition (1991) serves as a within-Quebec control for any inherent age-30 discontinuity.
  - Optional IV (Wald-RD): Use D as an instrument for the level of social assistance income (“other transfers”) to estimate the local effect of a $1 increase in benefits on labor supply for compliers.
- Control group(s)
  - Cross-sectional control: Rest of Canada (ROC) in 1986 (no age-30 discontinuity).
  - Temporal control: Quebec in 1991 (after removal, no discontinuity).
  - Combined: Difference-in-discontinuities = [Quebec 1986 jump at 30 − ROC 1986 jump] − [Quebec 1991 jump − ROC 1991 jump].
- Treatment timing / event date
  - The policy discontinuity exists up to July 1989; the 1986 Census captures the “on” regime. The 1991 Census captures the “off” regime (post-Aug 1989).
  - For the LFS event study: treatment removal on August 1, 1989.
- Running variable and cutoff (RDD)
  - Running variable: Age in single years (as of Census reference week).
  - Cutoff: 30th birthday (age ≥ 30 indicates higher-benefit eligibility pre-abolition).
  - Bandwidth: Local windows around 30 (e.g., ±3 to ±7 years), with robustness to bandwidth choice.

3. Key Identifying Assumptions
- Continuity of potential outcomes at age 30 absent the policy
  - In the absence of the age-30 benefit jump, employment, hours, living arrangements, and marital status should evolve smoothly through age 30. Plausibility: High. There are no well-known, discrete labor market or demographic changes that occur exactly at age 30 in Canada; any life-cycle transitions are gradual. Using ROC and the 1991 Quebec cross-section helps net out any spurious kinks at 30.
- No precise manipulation of the running variable
  - Individuals cannot sort their true age around 30 at the Census date; administrators verified age monthly for benefit classification, but reported age in the Census is not manipulable to gain benefits. Plausibility: Very high.
- No other Quebec-specific policy shifts that generate an independent age-30 discontinuity
  - Aside from social assistance, other age-indexed programs (e.g., medical/dental, UI) did not introduce a discrete jump at 30. Plausibility: High per institutional context.
- Stable composition around the threshold given conditioning
  - Conditioning on “childless” and “high school dropout” could, in principle, interact with age; however, the probability of having a child or completing education should be smooth through age 30. We will verify smoothness of observables at the cutoff.
- For the LFS DID/event study: common trends between 25–29 and 30–34 in Quebec relative to ROC in the absence of the 1989 change
  - Plausibility: Reasonable; we will test for pre-trend equivalence.

4. Threats to Identification and Mitigation
- Discrete age measurement and age heaping
  - Threat: Single-year-of-age creates a discrete running variable and potential coarser local control of age trends.
  - Mitigation: Use local linear (and quadratic) polynomials in age on either side within narrow bandwidths; implement alternative bandwidths (±3, ±4, ±5, ±7 years); placebo cutoffs (e.g., 28, 32); bias-corrected robust RD inference; cluster SEs appropriately (e.g., by age and province-year).
- Macroeconomic and cohort shocks (e.g., 1990–91 recession)
  - Threat: Quebec vs ROC or 1986 vs 1991 differences could confound estimates.
  - Mitigation: Identify effects via the discontinuity at age 30, not levels; use difference-in-discontinuities that net out Quebec×time shocks and age profiles; corroborate with LFS monthly event-study showing that the age-30 employment gap collapses right after Aug 1989 in Quebec relative to ROC.
- Concurrent policy changes targeted at young adults
  - Threat: Any Quebec-specific policy change at/near 30 unrelated to social assistance could contaminate estimates.
  - Mitigation: Document contemporaneous policies; test for discontinuities at 30 in ROC and in Quebec 1991; run placebo outcomes not plausibly affected by cash assistance (e.g., industry mix, education attainment conditional on dropout status) to check for unrelated discontinuities.

5. R Code Outline
Note: Replace file paths/variable names to match your master files. The code illustrates (i) difference-in-discontinuities around age 30 in Census microdata, (ii) a first-stage jump in transfers, (iii) a Wald-RD IV, and (iv) robustness checks.

# Packages
library(data.table)
library(fixest)        # fast high-dim FE and clustered SEs
library(sandwich)
library(lmtest)
library(rdrobust)      # optional RD diagnostics
library(ggplot2)

# 1) Load Census data (assume harmonized variable names across files)
c86 <- fread("census_1986.csv")
c91 <- fread("census_1991.csv")
c86[, year := 1986L]
c91[, year := 1991L]
c <- rbindlist(list(c86, c91), use.names = TRUE, fill = TRUE)

# 2) Sample restrictions
# Assume variables: sex (M/F), province (string), age (integer years),
# edu (categorical), dep_children (0/1 indicator of dependent children in hh),
# emp_current (0/1 current week employed), hours_week (numeric),
# weeks_last_year (numeric), earnings_last_year (numeric),
# ui_income (numeric), other_transfers (numeric),
# marital_status (levels), lives_with_parents (0/1)
# Define high school dropout: adjust to actual coding in your files
dropout_codes <- c("Less than high school", "No diploma")  # example
c <- c[
  sex == "M" &
    age >= 25 & age <= 39 &
    edu %in% dropout_codes &
    dep_children == 0 &
    province %in% c("Quebec", "Ontario", "British Columbia", "Alberta", "Manitoba",
                    "Saskatchewan", "New Brunswick", "Nova Scotia", "Prince Edward Island",
                    "Newfoundland and Labrador"),
  .(year, province, age, emp_current, hours_week, weeks_last_year, earnings_last_year,
    ui_income, other_transfers, marital_status, lives_with_parents)
]

# 3) Construct key variables
c[, que := as.integer(province == "Quebec")]
c[, roc := 1L - que]
c[, agec := age - 30]                 # centered running variable
c[, D := as.integer(age >= 30)]       # treatment-at-cutoff indicator
c[, pre := as.integer(year == 1986)]
c[, post := as.integer(year == 1991)]
c[, gy := interaction(que, year, drop = TRUE)] # group-year

# Optional trimming to local bandwidth (choose h; will vary in robustness)
h <- 5
clocal <- c[abs(agec) <= h]

# 4) Main specification: Difference-in-discontinuities around age 30
# Model: y ~ sum_g (tau_g * D_g) + piecewise age slopes by group-year
# where g indexes {Quebec 1986, Quebec 1991, ROC 1986, ROC 1991}.
# Implement by interacting D and age slopes with gy and "side" of cutoff.
clocal[, left := as.integer(age < 30)]
clocal[, right := 1L - left]

# Create side-specific age slopes by group-year
# Left slope
clocal[, agec_left := agec * left]
clocal[, agec_right := agec * right]

# Estimate for employment as primary outcome
m_emp <- feols(
  emp_current ~
    D:gy +                                 # discontinuity by group-year
    agec_left:gy + agec_right:gy,          # flexible local linear slopes by side x group-year
  data = clocal,
  cluster = c("age", "gy")                 # cluster by age and group-year
)

etable(m_emp)

# Extract the four discontinuities
# Names depend on factor coding; get coefficient names programmatically
coef_em <- coef(m_emp)
# Identify gy levels
levels_gy <- levels(clocal$gy)
print(levels_gy)
# Suppose levels_gy are: "0.1986"(ROC-1986), "0.1991"(ROC-1991), "1.1986"(Que-1986), "1.1991"(Que-1991)
# Build linear combinations:
# tau_Q86 - tau_ROC86 - (tau_Q91 - tau_ROC91)
lincom <- function(model, L, rhs = 0) wald(model, L = L, rhs = rhs)

Lnames <- names(coef_em)
# Helper to pick coefficient corresponding to D:gy==<level>
pick <- function(level) {
  nm <- paste0("D:gy", level)
  if (!nm %in% Lnames) stop("Coefficient name not found: ", nm)
  nm
}
# Build contrast matrix
L <- rep(0, length(coef_em)); names(L) <- Lnames
# Replace "0.1986", etc. by your levels
tau_Q86  <- pick("1.1986")
tau_ROC86<- pick("0.1986")
tau_Q91  <- pick("1.1991")
tau_ROC91<- pick("0.1991")

L1 <- L; L1[tau_Q86]   <-  1
L1[tau_ROC86]          <- -1
L1[tau_Q91]            <- -1
L1[tau_ROC91]          <-  1

did_rd_emp <- lincom(m_emp, L = rbind(DID_RD = L1))
did_rd_emp

# 5) First stage: jump in social assistance (proxied by 'other_transfers')
m_first <- feols(
  other_transfers ~ D:gy + agec_left:gy + agec_right:gy,
  data = clocal,
  cluster = c("age", "gy")
)
etable(m_first)

did_rd_first <- lincom(m_first, L = rbind(DID_RD = L1))
did_rd_first

# 6) Wald-RD IV (local LATE per $ of transfers)
# Stack equation with D:gy as excluded instrument; use iv_robust via fixest
m_iv <- feols(
  emp_current ~ agec_left:gy + agec_right:gy | (other_transfers ~ D:gy),
  data = clocal,
  cluster = c("age", "gy")
)
etable(m_iv)

# 7) Robustness checks
# a) Alternative bandwidths
for (hh in c(3,4,5,7)) {
  tmp <- c[abs(agec) <= hh]
  tmp[, left := as.integer(age < 30)]; tmp[, right := 1L - left]
  tmp[, agec_left := agec * left]; tmp[, agec_right := agec * right]
  mod <- feols(emp_current ~ D:gy + agec_left:gy + agec_right:gy, data = tmp, cluster = c("age","gy"))
  cat("\nBandwidth:", hh, "\n")
  print(lincom(mod, L = rbind(DID_RD = L1)))
}

# b) Placebo cutoffs at 28 and 32
placebo_test <- function(cut) {
  dt <- copy(c)
  dt[, agec := age - cut]
  dt <- dt[abs(agec) <= h]
  dt[, Dp := as.integer(age >= cut)]
  dt[, left := as.integer(age < cut)]
  dt[, right := 1L - left]
  dt[, agec_left := agec * left]
  dt[, agec_right := agec * right]
  m <- feols(emp_current ~ Dp:gy + agec_left:gy + agec_right:gy, data = dt, cluster = c("age","gy"))
  # Build contrast analogous to L1 but with Dp instead of D
  cn <- names(coef(m))
  getc <- function(level) paste0("Dp:gy", level)
  L <- rep(0, length(coef(m))); names(L) <- cn
  Lp <- L; Lp[getc("1.1986")] <- 1; Lp[getc("0.1986")] <- -1; Lp[getc("1.1991")] <- -1; Lp[getc("0.1991")] <- 1
  out <- lincom(m, L = rbind(DID_RD = Lp))
  list(cut = cut, res = out)
}
pl28 <- placebo_test(28)
pl32 <- placebo_test(32)
pl28; pl32

# c) RD density test (McCrary) at 30 using single-year-of-age frequencies
age_counts <- c[, .N, by = age][order(age)]
ggplot(age_counts, aes(x = age, y = N)) + geom_line() + geom_point() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 30, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(title = "Age distribution around 30", x = "Age", y = "Count")
# With single-year ages, formal McCrary is limited; visual check and counts suffice.

# d) Alternative outcomes: hours, weeks, living arrangements, marital status
m_hours <- feols(hours_week ~ D:gy + agec_left:gy + agec_right:gy, data = clocal, cluster = c("age","gy"))
m_weeks <- feols(weeks_last_year ~ D:gy + agec_left:gy + agec_right:gy, data = clocal, cluster = c("age","gy"))
m_livep <- feols(lives_with_parents ~ D:gy + agec_left:gy + agec_right:gy, data = clocal, cluster = c("age","gy"))
m_mar   <- feols(I(marital_status %in% c("Married","Common-law")) ~ D:gy + agec_left:gy + agec_right:gy,
                 data = clocal, cluster = c("age","gy"))

# e) Heterogeneity: narrow the sample to 27–33, 28–32, etc.
for (hh in c(2,3)) {
  tmp <- c[abs(age - 30) <= hh]
  tmp[, agec := age - 30]
  tmp[, left := as.integer(age < 30)]; tmp[, right := 1L - left]
  tmp[, agec_left := agec * left]; tmp[, agec_right := agec * right]
  mod <- feols(emp_current ~ D:gy + agec_left:gy + agec_right:gy, data = tmp, cluster = c("age","gy"))
  cat("\nNarrow window |age-30| <=", hh, "\n")
  print(lincom(mod, L = rbind(DID_RD = L1)))
}

# OPTIONAL: LFS DID/event study outline (requires monthly LFS file with age group 25–29, 30–34)
# Construct y (employment rate) by province-month-agegroup cells, then run:
# feols(emp_rate ~ i(rel_month, treat_group, ref = -1) + province*month_fe + province*agegroup_fe,
#       data = lfs_cells, cluster = province)


6. Expected Results
- Direction: More generous social assistance at age 30 should reduce current-week employment and weeks worked (income effect plus a 100% benefit reduction rate creating high implicit marginal tax rates). Hours conditional on employment may fall slightly or be unchanged; extensive margin should dominate.
- Magnitude (order-of-magnitude prior):
  - Employment: A discontinuity of −4 to −10 percentage points at age 30 in Quebec in 1986 relative to appropriate controls seems plausible given a ~$322/month jump ($507−$185) or ~$3,864/year and very high tax-back rates.
  - Weeks worked: −2 to −6 weeks annually.
  - Living arrangements: With higher benefits at 30, co-residence with parents likely falls modestly (greater ability to live independently).
  - Marital/common-law: Modest decline in partnership formation incentives at 30 (benefits targeted to singles) could induce a small drop in marriage/common-law rates near the cutoff.

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment
- C1: Running variable not manipulable at the cutoff (age) — 1
- C2: Potential outcomes smooth in age absent treatment (tested via ROC and 1991 placebos) — 1
- C3: Correct local specification and bandwidth choice (local linear with side-specific slopes; multiple bandwidths; placebo cutoffs) — 1
- C4: No other policies/treatments discontinuous at age 30 that differentially affect Quebec vs ROC or 1986 vs 1991 — 1
- C5: Stable composition around the cutoff within the analysis sample (check smoothness of observables; verify no discontinuity in covariates/density) — 1

Notes and implementation details
- Use survey weights if provided in master files; the code above treats observations as unweighted—add weights = w in feols if needed.
- Clustered SEs: Because treatment varies at the age-year-province level, clustering by age and group-year is conservative; alternative clustering (e.g., by age only) can be shown for robustness.
- Scaling to elasticities: If desired, divide reduced-form effects by the benefit jump to produce semi-elasticities per $100 of benefits, or compute a Wald-RD IV using the first-stage in other_transfers.
- Measurement of “other transfers”: Confirm that this category predominantly captures social assistance in your subsample; exclude UI or control for ui_income to isolate SA.
